Step 4 · Board questions

Sample paper and case-study questions

18 questions from official CBSE sources. Each answer has two views: Understand it (every step) and Write it in the exam (what earns the marks).

Past board papers not yet available — to be added. This section currently holds the Introduction to Trigonometry items from the CBSE Mathematics Sample Question Papers 2026-27 and 2025-26 — Mathematics Standard (041) and Mathematics Basic (241) — answered with their official marking schemes (newest first). Past year board questions, and the "Exam focus" analysis, will be added once the papers are sourced. Heights-and-distances items from the same papers belong to Chapter 9.

Both 2026-27 SQPs state that there is no change in the question paper design and assessment pattern for 2026-27, so the 2025-26 items remain good practice. Standard and Basic share the same syllabus, so every student should try all eighteen items.

Each item has two parts:

  • Understand it — the full step-by-step explanation: Given / Asked → Concept used (and why) → steps → Check → answer → Common trap.
  • Write it in the exam — the answer as you should write it, following the official marking scheme, with marks shown. Where the scheme gives only a total, the split shown is inferred and marked so.

CBSE Sample Question Paper 2026-27

CBSE SQP 2026-27, Mathematics Standard, Section A, Q81 mark

Question: If tan⁡(A+B)=3\tan(A + B) = \sqrt{3}tan(A+B)=3​ and tan⁡(A−B)=13\tan(A - B) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}tan(A−B)=3​1​, 0°<A+B<90°0° < A + B < 90°0°<A+B<90°, A>BA > BA>B, then the value of A and B respectively are:

Given: tan⁡(A+B)=3\tan(A + B) = \sqrt{3}tan(A+B)=3​, tan⁡(A−B)=13\tan(A - B) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}tan(A−B)=3​1​. Asked: A and B.

Concept used: read each bracket as one angle from the table; then solve two linear equations (Topic 4). Why it applies: 3\sqrt{3}3​ and 13\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}3​1​ are both table values of tan. (A > B makes A−BA - BA−B positive.)

  1. 1

    tan⁡60°=3\tan 60° = \sqrt{3}tan60°=3​.

    A+B=60°…(1)A + B = 60° \quad \text{…(1)}A+B=60°…(1)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    tan⁡30°=13\tan 30° = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}tan30°=3​1​.

    A−B=30°…(2)A - B = 30° \quad \text{…(2)}A−B=30°…(2)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Add (1) and (2).

    2A=90°2A = 90°2A=90°Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Divide by 2.

    A=45°A = 45°A=45°Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Substitute into (1).

    B=60°−45°=15°B = 60° - 45° = 15°B=60°−45°=15°Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    A = 45°, B = 15° → option C.

  7. Check: tan⁡(45°+15°)=tan⁡60°=3\tan(45° + 15°) = \tan 60° = \sqrt{3}tan(45°+15°)=tan60°=3​ ✔; tan⁡(45°−15°)=tan⁡30°=13\tan(45° - 15°) = \tan 30° = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}tan(45°−15°)=tan30°=3​1​ ✔.

    Why the other options are wrong: A gives A+B=90°A + B = 90°A+B=90°, where tan is not defined. B gives A+B=105°A + B = 105°A+B=105°, outside the given range. D gives A+B=75°A + B = 75°A+B=75°, and tan⁡75°≠3\tan 75° \neq \sqrt{3}tan75°=3​.
    Common trap: Mixing up tan⁡30°\tan 30°tan30° and tan⁡60°\tan 60°tan60° — that gives A+B=30°A + B = 30°A+B=30° and A−B=60°A - B = 60°A−B=60°, so B would come out negative.
(C) 45°, 15°. tan⁡(A+B)=3\tan(A + B) = \sqrt{3}tan(A+B)=3​, so A+B=60°A + B = 60°A+B=60° …(i). tan⁡(A−B)=13\tan(A - B) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}tan(A−B)=3​1​, so A−B=30°A - B = 30°A−B=30° …(ii). Solving (i) and (ii), A=45°A = 45°A=45° and B=15°B = 15°B=15°
1 mark
CBSE SQP 2026-27, Mathematics Standard, Section B, Q232 marks

Question: If tan⁡θ=15\tan\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}tanθ=5​1​, then find the value of cosec⁡2θ−sec⁡2θcosec⁡2θ+sec⁡2θ\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta - \sec^2\theta}{\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta + \sec^2\theta}cosec2θ+sec2θcosec2θ−sec2θ​.

Given: tan⁡θ=15\tan\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}tanθ=5​1​. Asked: the value of the expression.

Concept used: the identities sec⁡2θ=1+tan⁡2θ\sec^2\theta = 1 + \tan^2\thetasec2θ=1+tan2θ and cosec⁡2θ=1+cot⁡2θ\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta = 1 + \cot^2\thetacosec2θ=1+cot2θ (Topic 5). Why it applies: both squares in the expression can be found straight from tan⁡θ\tan\thetatanθ and cot⁡θ\cot\thetacotθ.

  1. 1

    cot is the reciprocal of tan.

    cot⁡θ=5\cot\theta = \sqrt{5}cotθ=5​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Find sec⁡2θ\sec^2\thetasec2θ.

    sec⁡2θ=1+tan⁡2θ=1+(15)2=1+15=65\sec^2\theta = 1 + \tan^2\theta = 1 + \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\right)^2 = 1 + \dfrac{1}{5} = \dfrac{6}{5}sec2θ=1+tan2θ=1+(5​1​)2=1+51​=56​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Find cosec⁡2θ\operatorname{cosec}^2\thetacosec2θ.

    cosec⁡2θ=1+cot⁡2θ=1+(5)2=1+5=6\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta = 1 + \cot^2\theta = 1 + (\sqrt{5})^2 = 1 + 5 = 6cosec2θ=1+cot2θ=1+(5​)2=1+5=6Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Substitute into the expression.

    6−656+65\dfrac{6 - \dfrac{6}{5}}{6 + \dfrac{6}{5}}6+56​6−56​​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Work out top and bottom: 6−65=2456 - \dfrac{6}{5} = \dfrac{24}{5}6−56​=524​ and 6+65=3656 + \dfrac{6}{5} = \dfrac{36}{5}6+56​=536​.

    =  245    365  = \dfrac{\;\dfrac{24}{5}\;}{\;\dfrac{36}{5}\;}=536​524​​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    The fifths cancel.

    =2436=23= \dfrac{24}{36} = \dfrac{2}{3}=3624​=32​Swipe to see the whole equation →

  7. Check (another way, optional): multiply top and bottom by sin⁡2θ\sin^2\thetasin2θ: cosec⁡2θsin⁡2θ=1\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta \sin^2\theta = 1cosec2θsin2θ=1 and sec⁡2θsin⁡2θ=tan⁡2θ\sec^2\theta\sin^2\theta = \tan^2\thetasec2θsin2θ=tan2θ, so the expression is 1−tan⁡2θ1+tan⁡2θ=1−151+15=46=23\dfrac{1 - \tan^2\theta}{1 + \tan^2\theta} = \dfrac{1 - \dfrac{1}{5}}{1 + \dfrac{1}{5}} = \dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{2}{3}1+tan2θ1−tan2θ​=1+51​1−51​​=64​=32​ ✔.

  8. Answer 23\dfrac{2}{3}32​

    Common trap: Writing sec⁡2θ=1+15\sec^2\theta = 1 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}sec2θ=1+5​1​ — forgetting to square 15\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}5​1​. Its square is 15\dfrac{1}{5}51​.
tan⁡θ=15⇒cot⁡θ=5\tan\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \Rightarrow \cot\theta = \sqrt{5}tanθ=5​1​⇒cotθ=5​; sec⁡2θ=1+tan⁡2θ=1+(15)2=65\sec^2\theta = 1 + \tan^2\theta = 1 + \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\right)^2 = \dfrac{6}{5}sec2θ=1+tan2θ=1+(5​1​)2=56​
½ mark
cosec⁡2θ=1+cot⁡2θ=1+(5)2=6\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta = 1 + \cot^2\theta = 1 + (\sqrt{5})^2 = 6cosec2θ=1+cot2θ=1+(5​)2=6
½ mark
∴cosec⁡2θ−sec⁡2θcosec⁡2θ+sec⁡2θ=6−656+65=23\therefore \dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta - \sec^2\theta}{\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta + \sec^2\theta} = \dfrac{6 - \dfrac{6}{5}}{6 + \dfrac{6}{5}} = \dfrac{2}{3}∴cosec2θ+sec2θcosec2θ−sec2θ​=6+56​6−56​​=32​
1 mark
CBSE SQP 2026-27, Mathematics Standard, Section C, Q31 (A)3 marks

Question: During a math class, Ms. Isha wrote the expression given below on the board and asked the students to simplify it.

cos⁡θ1−sin⁡θ+1−sin⁡θcos⁡θ\dfrac{\cos\theta}{1 - \sin\theta} + \dfrac{1 - \sin\theta}{\cos\theta}1−sinθcosθ​+cosθ1−sinθ​Swipe to see the whole equation →

Jyoti solved it in her note book as follows:

cos⁡θ1−sin⁡θ+1−sin⁡θcos⁡θ\dfrac{\cos\theta}{1 - \sin\theta} + \dfrac{1 - \sin\theta}{\cos\theta}1−sinθcosθ​+cosθ1−sinθ​Swipe to see the whole equation →
=cos⁡2θ+(1−sin⁡θ)2(1−sin⁡θ)×cos⁡θ…(step 1)= \dfrac{\cos^2\theta + (1 - \sin\theta)^2}{(1 - \sin\theta) \times \cos\theta} \quad \text{…(step 1)}=(1−sinθ)×cosθcos2θ+(1−sinθ)2​…(step 1)Swipe to see the whole equation →
=cos⁡2θ+cos⁡2θ(1−sin⁡θ)×cos⁡θ…(step 2)= \dfrac{\cos^2\theta + \cos^2\theta}{(1 - \sin\theta) \times \cos\theta} \quad \text{…(step 2)}=(1−sinθ)×cosθcos2θ+cos2θ​…(step 2)Swipe to see the whole equation →
=2cos⁡2θ(1−sin⁡θ)×cos⁡θ…(step 3)= \dfrac{2\cos^2\theta}{(1 - \sin\theta) \times \cos\theta} \quad \text{…(step 3)}=(1−sinθ)×cosθ2cos2θ​…(step 3)Swipe to see the whole equation →
=2cos⁡θ1−sin⁡θ…(step 4)= \dfrac{2\cos\theta}{1 - \sin\theta} \quad \text{…(step 4)}=1−sinθ2cosθ​…(step 4)Swipe to see the whole equation →

Identify the step in which Jyoti has made error(s), if any. Rectify the same and find the correct answer.

Given: the expression and Jyoti's four steps. Asked: the wrong step, the correction, and the correct answer.

Concept used: Move 2 (add fractions with an LCM), then expand a square and use Move 4 (sin⁡2θ+cos⁡2θ=1\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1sin2θ+cos2θ=1) (Topics 5 and 6). Why it applies: checking each step against these rules finds the error.

  1. 1

    Finding the error

    Step 1: LCM of the bottoms is (1−sin⁡θ)cos⁡θ(1 - \sin\theta)\cos\theta(1−sinθ)cosθ; the tops become cos⁡θ×cos⁡θ\cos\theta \times \cos\thetacosθ×cosθ and (1−sin⁡θ)(1−sin⁡θ)(1 - \sin\theta)(1 - \sin\theta)(1−sinθ)(1−sinθ). Correct.

  2. 2

    Step 2: Jyoti replaced (1−sin⁡θ)2(1 - \sin\theta)^2(1−sinθ)2 by cos⁡2θ\cos^2\thetacos2θ. But the identity says cos⁡2θ=1−sin⁡2θ\cos^2\theta = 1 - \sin^2\thetacos2θ=1−sin2θ, which is not the same as (1−sin⁡θ)2(1 - \sin\theta)^2(1−sinθ)2. Step 2 is wrong.

  3. 3

    Steps 3 and 4 are built on step 2, so her final answer is wrong too.

  4. 4

    Correct working

    Start from step 1, which was right.

    cos⁡2θ+(1−sin⁡θ)2(1−sin⁡θ)cos⁡θ\dfrac{\cos^2\theta + (1 - \sin\theta)^2}{(1 - \sin\theta)\cos\theta}(1−sinθ)cosθcos2θ+(1−sinθ)2​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Expand (1−sin⁡θ)2=1−2sin⁡θ+sin⁡2θ(1 - \sin\theta)^2 = 1 - 2\sin\theta + \sin^2\theta(1−sinθ)2=1−2sinθ+sin2θ.

    =cos⁡2θ+1−2sin⁡θ+sin⁡2θ(1−sin⁡θ)cos⁡θ= \dfrac{\cos^2\theta + 1 - 2\sin\theta + \sin^2\theta}{(1 - \sin\theta)\cos\theta}=(1−sinθ)cosθcos2θ+1−2sinθ+sin2θ​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Move 4: sin⁡2θ+cos⁡2θ=1\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1sin2θ+cos2θ=1, so the top becomes 1+1−2sin⁡θ1 + 1 - 2\sin\theta1+1−2sinθ.

    =2−2sin⁡θ(1−sin⁡θ)cos⁡θ= \dfrac{2 - 2\sin\theta}{(1 - \sin\theta)\cos\theta}=(1−sinθ)cosθ2−2sinθ​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Take out the common factor 2 on top.

    =2(1−sin⁡θ)(1−sin⁡θ)cos⁡θ= \dfrac{2(1 - \sin\theta)}{(1 - \sin\theta)\cos\theta}=(1−sinθ)cosθ2(1−sinθ)​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Cancel (1−sin⁡θ)(1 - \sin\theta)(1−sinθ).

    =2cos⁡θ= \dfrac{2}{\cos\theta}=cosθ2​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  9. 9

    Reciprocal: 1cos⁡θ=sec⁡θ\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} = \sec\thetacosθ1​=secθ.

    =2sec⁡θ= 2\sec\theta=2secθSwipe to see the whole equation →

  10. Check: at θ = 30°: cos⁡30°1−sin⁡30°+1−sin⁡30°cos⁡30°=3/21/2+1/23/2=3+13=43\dfrac{\cos 30°}{1 - \sin 30°} + \dfrac{1 - \sin 30°}{\cos 30°} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}/2}{1/2} + \dfrac{1/2}{\sqrt{3}/2} = \sqrt{3} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{4}{\sqrt{3}}1−sin30°cos30°​+cos30°1−sin30°​=1/23​/2​+3​/21/2​=3​+3​1​=3​4​, and 2sec⁡30°=2×23=432\sec 30° = 2 \times \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{4}{\sqrt{3}}2sec30°=2×3​2​=3​4​ ✔. Jyoti's answer gives 2×3/21/2=23\dfrac{2 \times \sqrt{3}/2}{1/2} = 2\sqrt{3}1/22×3​/2​=23​, which does not match.

  11. Answer The error is in step 2; the correct value is 2sec⁡θ2\sec\theta2secθ.

    Common trap: Jyoti's own mistake — treating (1−sin⁡θ)2(1 - \sin\theta)^2(1−sinθ)2 as 1−sin⁡2θ1 - \sin^2\theta1−sin2θ. Squaring a bracket gives three terms: 1−2sin⁡θ+sin⁡2θ1 - 2\sin\theta + \sin^2\theta1−2sinθ+sin2θ.
Jyoti made an error in step 2.
1 mark
Correct solution: cos⁡θ1−sin⁡θ+1−sin⁡θcos⁡θ=cos⁡2θ+(1−sin⁡θ)2(1−sin⁡θ)cos⁡θ=cos⁡2θ+1+sin⁡2θ−2sin⁡θ(1−sin⁡θ)cos⁡θ\dfrac{\cos\theta}{1 - \sin\theta} + \dfrac{1 - \sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \dfrac{\cos^2\theta + (1 - \sin\theta)^2}{(1 - \sin\theta)\cos\theta} = \dfrac{\cos^2\theta + 1 + \sin^2\theta - 2\sin\theta}{(1 - \sin\theta)\cos\theta}1−sinθcosθ​+cosθ1−sinθ​=(1−sinθ)cosθcos2θ+(1−sinθ)2​=(1−sinθ)cosθcos2θ+1+sin2θ−2sinθ​
1 mark
=2−2sin⁡θ(1−sin⁡θ)cos⁡θ= \dfrac{2 - 2\sin\theta}{(1 - \sin\theta)\cos\theta}=(1−sinθ)cosθ2−2sinθ​
½ mark
=2(1−sin⁡θ)(1−sin⁡θ)cos⁡θ=2cos⁡θ=2sec⁡θ= \dfrac{2(1 - \sin\theta)}{(1 - \sin\theta)\cos\theta} = \dfrac{2}{\cos\theta} = 2\sec\theta=(1−sinθ)cosθ2(1−sinθ)​=cosθ2​=2secθ
½ mark
CBSE SQP 2026-27, Mathematics Standard, Section C, Q31 (B)3 marks

Question: If 1sin⁡x−cos⁡x=cosec⁡x2\dfrac{1}{\sin x - \cos x} = \dfrac{\operatorname{cosec} x}{\sqrt{2}}sinx−cosx1​=2​cosecx​, then prove that (1sin⁡x+cos⁡x)2=sec⁡2x2\left(\dfrac{1}{\sin x + \cos x}\right)^2 = \dfrac{\sec^2 x}{2}(sinx+cosx1​)2=2sec2x​.

Given: 1sin⁡x−cos⁡x=cosec⁡x2\dfrac{1}{\sin x - \cos x} = \dfrac{\operatorname{cosec} x}{\sqrt{2}}sinx−cosx1​=2​cosecx​. To prove: (1sin⁡x+cos⁡x)2=sec⁡2x2\left(\dfrac{1}{\sin x + \cos x}\right)^2 = \dfrac{\sec^2 x}{2}(sinx+cosx1​)2=2sec2x​.

Concept used: turn the given condition into a relation for 2sin⁡xcos⁡x2\sin x\cos x2sinxcosx by squaring and using sin⁡2x+cos⁡2x=1\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1sin2x+cos2x=1; then expand (sin⁡x+cos⁡x)2(\sin x + \cos x)^2(sinx+cosx)2, which contains the same 2sin⁡xcos⁡x2\sin x\cos x2sinxcosx (Topics 5 and 6). Why it applies: (sin⁡x−cos⁡x)2(\sin x - \cos x)^2(sinx−cosx)2 and (sin⁡x+cos⁡x)2(\sin x + \cos x)^2(sinx+cosx)2 both equal "1 ∓ 2sin⁡xcos⁡x2\sin x\cos x2sinxcosx".

  1. 1

    From the given condition

    Move 1: cosec⁡x=1sin⁡x\operatorname{cosec} x = \dfrac{1}{\sin x}cosecx=sinx1​, so the right side is 12sin⁡x\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\sin x}2​sinx1​.

    1sin⁡x−cos⁡x=12sin⁡x\dfrac{1}{\sin x - \cos x} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\sin x}sinx−cosx1​=2​sinx1​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Both fractions have top 1, so their bottoms are equal.

    sin⁡x−cos⁡x=2sin⁡x\sin x - \cos x = \sqrt{2}\sin xsinx−cosx=2​sinxSwipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Square both sides (it is an equation, so both sides may change).

    sin⁡2x−2sin⁡xcos⁡x+cos⁡2x=2sin⁡2x\sin^2 x - 2\sin x\cos x + \cos^2 x = 2\sin^2 xsin2x−2sinxcosx+cos2x=2sin2xSwipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Move 4: sin⁡2x+cos⁡2x=1\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1sin2x+cos2x=1.

    1−2sin⁡xcos⁡x=2sin⁡2x1 - 2\sin x\cos x = 2\sin^2 x1−2sinxcosx=2sin2xSwipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Rearrange to get 2sin⁡xcos⁡x2\sin x\cos x2sinxcosx on its own.

    2sin⁡xcos⁡x=1−2sin⁡2x…(i)2\sin x\cos x = 1 - 2\sin^2 x \quad \text{…(i)}2sinxcosx=1−2sin2x…(i)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Now the proof

    Start from the LHS.

    LHS=(1sin⁡x+cos⁡x)2=1(sin⁡x+cos⁡x)2\text{LHS} = \left(\dfrac{1}{\sin x + \cos x}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{(\sin x + \cos x)^2}LHS=(sinx+cosx1​)2=(sinx+cosx)21​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Expand the bottom and use Move 4.

    =1sin⁡2x+2sin⁡xcos⁡x+cos⁡2x=11+2sin⁡xcos⁡x= \dfrac{1}{\sin^2 x + 2\sin x\cos x + \cos^2 x} = \dfrac{1}{1 + 2\sin x\cos x}=sin2x+2sinxcosx+cos2x1​=1+2sinxcosx1​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Substitute (i).

    =11+(1−2sin⁡2x)=12−2sin⁡2x= \dfrac{1}{1 + (1 - 2\sin^2 x)} = \dfrac{1}{2 - 2\sin^2 x}=1+(1−2sin2x)1​=2−2sin2x1​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  9. 9

    Take out 2 and use Move 4 again: 1−sin⁡2x=cos⁡2x1 - \sin^2 x = \cos^2 x1−sin2x=cos2x.

    =12(1−sin⁡2x)=12cos⁡2x= \dfrac{1}{2(1 - \sin^2 x)} = \dfrac{1}{2\cos^2 x}=2(1−sin2x)1​=2cos2x1​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  10. 10

    Move 1: 1cos⁡2x=sec⁡2x\dfrac{1}{\cos^2 x} = \sec^2 xcos2x1​=sec2x.

    =sec⁡2x2=RHS= \dfrac{\sec^2 x}{2} = \text{RHS}=2sec2x​=RHSSwipe to see the whole equation →

    Hence proved.

    A note for curious students (not needed in the exam): no acute angle actually satisfies the given condition. Step 2 rearranges to cos⁡x=(1−2)sin⁡x\cos x = (1 - \sqrt{2})\sin xcosx=(1−2​)sinx. For an acute angle cos⁡x\cos xcosx is positive, but (1−2)sin⁡x(1 - \sqrt{2})\sin x(1−2​)sinx is negative (because 2>1\sqrt{2} > 12​>1). Angles that do satisfy it are bigger than 90°, which you will meet in Class 11. The question tests the algebra of "if this, then that", and the marking scheme awards marks for exactly the steps above.

    Common trap: Squaring (sin⁡x−cos⁡x)(\sin x - \cos x)(sinx−cosx) as sin⁡2x−cos⁡2x\sin^2 x - \cos^2 xsin2x−cos2x. A squared bracket has a middle term: −2sin⁡xcos⁡x-2\sin x\cos x−2sinxcosx.
Given 1sin⁡x−cos⁡x=cosec⁡x2⇒sin⁡x−cos⁡x=2sin⁡x\dfrac{1}{\sin x - \cos x} = \dfrac{\operatorname{cosec} x}{\sqrt{2}} \Rightarrow \sin x - \cos x = \sqrt{2}\sin xsinx−cosx1​=2​cosecx​⇒sinx−cosx=2​sinx
½ mark
Squaring both sides, 2sin⁡xcos⁡x=1−2sin⁡2x2\sin x\cos x = 1 - 2\sin^2 x2sinxcosx=1−2sin2x …(i)
1 mark
Now, LHS =(1sin⁡x+cos⁡x)2=11+2sin⁡xcos⁡x= \left(\dfrac{1}{\sin x + \cos x}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{1 + 2\sin x\cos x}=(sinx+cosx1​)2=1+2sinxcosx1​
½ mark
=11+(1−2sin⁡2x)=12cos⁡2x= \dfrac{1}{1 + (1 - 2\sin^2 x)} = \dfrac{1}{2\cos^2 x}=1+(1−2sin2x)1​=2cos2x1​
½ mark
=sec⁡2x2== \dfrac{\sec^2 x}{2} ==2sec2x​= RHS

Question: The value of sin⁡260°−2tan⁡245°−cos⁡230°\sin^2 60° - 2\tan^2 45° - \cos^2 30°sin260°−2tan245°−cos230° is

Given: an expression in table values. Asked: its value.

Concept used: substitute from the table of values and square each value (Topic 4). Why it applies: all three angles are standard angles.

  1. 1

    Values: sin⁡60°=32\sin 60° = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}sin60°=23​​, tan⁡45°=1\tan 45° = 1tan45°=1, cos⁡30°=32\cos 30° = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}cos30°=23​​.

  2. 2

    Substitute.

    (32)2−2(1)2−(32)2\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2 - 2(1)^2 - \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2(23​​)2−2(1)2−(23​​)2Swipe to see the whole equation →

Given: sec⁡θ+tan⁡θ=x\sec\theta + \tan\theta = xsecθ+tanθ=x. Asked: sec⁡θ−tan⁡θ\sec\theta - \tan\thetasecθ−tanθ.

Concept used: (sec⁡θ−tan⁡θ)(sec⁡θ+tan⁡θ)=sec⁡2θ−tan⁡2θ=1(\sec\theta - \tan\theta)(\sec\theta + \tan\theta) = \sec^2\theta - \tan^2\theta = 1(secθ−tanθ)(secθ+tanθ)=sec2θ−tan2θ=1 (Topic 5). Why it applies: the sum and the difference multiply to 1, so each is the reciprocal of the other.

  1. 1

    Write the identity in bracket form.

    (sec⁡θ−tan⁡θ)(sec⁡θ+tan⁡θ)=1(\sec\theta - \tan\theta)(\sec\theta + \tan\theta) = 1(secθ−tanθ)(secθ+tanθ)=1Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Substitute sec⁡θ+tan⁡θ=x\sec\theta + \tan\theta = xsecθ+tanθ=x.

    (sec⁡θ−tan⁡θ)×x=1(\sec\theta - \tan\theta) \times x = 1(secθ−tanθ)×x=1Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Divide by xxx.

    sec⁡θ−tan⁡θ=1x\sec\theta - \tan\theta = \dfrac{1}{x}secθ−tanθ=x1​Swipe to see the whole equation →

    Why the other options are wrong: A assumes the difference equals the sum; B and C have no identity behind them.
    Common trap: Writing sec⁡θ−tan⁡θ=1−x\sec\theta - \tan\theta = 1 - xsecθ−tanθ=1−x by misusing sec⁡2θ−tan⁡2θ=1\sec^2\theta - \tan^2\theta = 1sec2θ−tan2θ=1 without the squares.
D. 1x\dfrac{1}{x}x1​, since 1sec⁡θ+tan⁡θ=sec⁡θ−tan⁡θsec⁡2θ−tan⁡2θ=sec⁡θ−tan⁡θ\dfrac{1}{\sec\theta + \tan\theta} = \dfrac{\sec\theta - \tan\theta}{\sec^2\theta - \tan^2\theta} = \sec\theta - \tan\thetasecθ+tanθ1​=sec2θ−tan2θsecθ−tanθ​=secθ−tanθ

Concept used: rearrange the given condition and use sin⁡2A=1−cos⁡2A\sin^2 A = 1 - \cos^2 Asin2A=1−cos2A (Topic 5). Why it applies: the condition can be rewritten to give cos⁡A=sin⁡2A\cos A = \sin^2 AcosA=sin2A.

    Use R: 1−cos⁡2A=sin⁡2A1 - \cos^2 A = \sin^2 A1−cos2A=sin2A.

Why it applies: both the condition and the target can be expressed through the product sin⁡θcos⁡θ\sin\theta\cos\thetasinθcosθ.

    Square both sides of the given condition (it is an equation, so both sides may change).

  2. 2

    Expand.

    sin⁡2θ+2sin⁡θcos⁡θ+cos⁡2θ=3\sin^2\theta + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta + \cos^2\theta = 3sin2θ+2sinθcosθ+cos2θ=3Swipe to see the whole equation →

  4. 4

    Subtract 1 from both sides.

    2sin⁡θcos⁡θ=22\sin\theta\cos\theta = 22sinθcosθ=2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Divide both sides by 2.

    sin⁡θcos⁡θ=1\sin\theta\cos\theta = 1sinθcosθ=1Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Now simplify the expression to be found. Move 1:

    tan⁡θ+cot⁡θ=sin⁡θcos⁡θ+cos⁡θsin⁡θ\tan\theta + \cot\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} + \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}tanθ+cotθ=cosθsinθ​+sinθcosθ​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Move 2 (LCM).

    =sin⁡2θ+cos⁡2θsin⁡θcos⁡θ= \dfrac{\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}=sinθcosθsin2θ+cos2θ​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Move 4.

    =1sin⁡θcos⁡θ= \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}=sinθcosθ1​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  9. 9

    Substitute sin⁡θcos⁡θ=1\sin\theta\cos\theta = 1sinθcosθ=1 from step 5.

    =11=1= \dfrac{1}{1} = 1=11​=1Swipe to see the whole equation →

    Hence proved.

    A note for curious students (not needed in the exam): no real angle actually satisfies sin⁡θ+cos⁡θ=3\sin\theta + \cos\theta = \sqrt{3}sinθ+cosθ=3​. Here is why: (sin⁡θ−cos⁡θ)2≥0(\sin\theta - \cos\theta)^2 \geq 0(sinθ−cosθ)2≥0 gives 1−2sin⁡θcos⁡θ≥01 - 2\sin\theta\cos\theta \geq 01−2sinθcosθ≥0, so sin⁡θcos⁡θ≤12\sin\theta\cos\theta \leq \dfrac{1}{2}sinθcosθ≤21​. Step 5 needs sin⁡θcos⁡θ=1\sin\theta\cos\theta = 1sinθcosθ=1, which is impossible. In the same way, (sin⁡θ+cos⁡θ)2=1+2sin⁡θcos⁡θ≤2(\sin\theta + \cos\theta)^2 = 1 + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta \leq 2(sinθ+cosθ)2=1+2sinθcosθ≤2, so sin⁡θ+cos⁡θ\sin\theta + \cos\thetasinθ+cosθ can never be more than 2\sqrt{2}2​. The question tests the algebra of "if this, then that", and the marking scheme awards marks for exactly the steps above.

    Common trap: Squaring and writing (sin⁡θ+cos⁡θ)2=sin⁡2θ+cos⁡2θ=1(\sin\theta + \cos\theta)^2 = \sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1(sinθ+cosθ)2=sin2θ+cos2θ=1, which loses the 2sin⁡θcos⁡θ2\sin\theta\cos\theta2sinθcosθ term and gives "1=31 = 31=3".

Question: Prove that cos⁡A−sin⁡A+1cos⁡A+sin⁡A−1=cosec⁡A+cot⁡A\dfrac{\cos A - \sin A + 1}{\cos A + \sin A - 1} = \operatorname{cosec} A + \cot AcosA+sinA−1cosA−sinA+1​=cosecA+cotA.

Given: the identity. To prove: LHS = RHS.

Concept used: Move 3 — multiply top and bottom by (cos⁡A+sin⁡A+1)(\cos A + \sin A + 1)(cosA+sinA+1), so that the bottom becomes (cos⁡A+sin⁡A)2−1(\cos A + \sin A)^2 - 1(cosA+sinA)2−1; then Move 4 and Move 5 (Topic 6). Why it applies: the bottom is "something minus 1", and multiplying by "the same something plus 1" gives a difference of squares. (This is the marking-scheme method — a 3-move "Challenge" proof.)

  1. 1

    Start from the LHS.

    LHS=cos⁡A−sin⁡A+1cos⁡A+sin⁡A−1\text{LHS} = \dfrac{\cos A - \sin A + 1}{\cos A + \sin A - 1}LHS=cosA+sinA−1cosA−sinA+1​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Move 3: multiply top and bottom by (cos⁡A+sin⁡A+1)(\cos A + \sin A + 1)(cosA+sinA+1).

    =(cos⁡A−sin⁡A+1)(cos⁡A+sin⁡A+1)(cos⁡A+sin⁡A−1)(cos⁡A+sin⁡A+1)= \dfrac{(\cos A - \sin A + 1)(\cos A + \sin A + 1)}{(\cos A + \sin A - 1)(\cos A + \sin A + 1)}=(cosA+sinA−1)(cosA+sinA+1)(cosA−sinA+1)(cosA+sinA+1)​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Top: group as [(cos⁡A+1)−sin⁡A][(cos⁡A+1)+sin⁡A]=(cos⁡A+1)2−sin⁡2A[(\cos A + 1) - \sin A][(\cos A + 1) + \sin A] = (\cos A + 1)^2 - \sin^2 A[(cosA+1)−sinA][(cosA+1)+sinA]=(cosA+1)2−sin2A. Bottom: (cos⁡A+sin⁡A)2−1(\cos A + \sin A)^2 - 1(cosA+sinA)2−1.

    =(cos⁡A+1)2−sin⁡2A(cos⁡A+sin⁡A)2−1= \dfrac{(\cos A + 1)^2 - \sin^2 A}{(\cos A + \sin A)^2 - 1}=(cosA+sinA)2−1(cosA+1)2−sin2A​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Expand both squares.

    =cos⁡2A+2cos⁡A+1−sin⁡2Acos⁡2A+2sin⁡Acos⁡A+sin⁡2A−1= \dfrac{\cos^2 A + 2\cos A + 1 - \sin^2 A}{\cos^2 A + 2\sin A\cos A + \sin^2 A - 1}=cos2A+2sinAcosA+sin2A−1cos2A+2cosA+1−sin2A​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Move 4: on top, 1−sin⁡2A=cos⁡2A1 - \sin^2 A = \cos^2 A1−sin2A=cos2A; on the bottom, cos⁡2A+sin⁡2A−1=0\cos^2 A + \sin^2 A - 1 = 0cos2A+sin2A−1=0.

    =2cos⁡2A+2cos⁡A2sin⁡Acos⁡A= \dfrac{2\cos^2 A + 2\cos A}{2\sin A\cos A}=2sinAcosA2cos2A+2cosA​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Move 5: take out 2cos⁡A2\cos A2cosA on top.

    =2cos⁡A (cos⁡A+1)2sin⁡Acos⁡A= \dfrac{2\cos A\,(\cos A + 1)}{2\sin A\cos A}=2sinAcosA2cosA(cosA+1)​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Cancel 2cos⁡A2\cos A2cosA.

    =1+cos⁡Asin⁡A= \dfrac{1 + \cos A}{\sin A}=sinA1+cosA​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Split.

    =1sin⁡A+cos⁡Asin⁡A=cosec⁡A+cot⁡A=RHS= \dfrac{1}{\sin A} + \dfrac{\cos A}{\sin A} = \operatorname{cosec} A + \cot A = \text{RHS}=sinA1​+sinAcosA​=cosecA+cotA=RHSSwipe to see the whole equation →

  9. Hence proved.

    Check: at A = 60°: LHS =3= \sqrt{3}=3​ and RHS =23+13=3= \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \sqrt{3}=3​2​+3​1​=3​ ✔.

    Common trap: Multiplying only the bottom by (cos⁡A+sin⁡A+1)(\cos A + \sin A + 1)(cosA+sinA+1). Top and bottom must both be multiplied.
cos⁡A−sin⁡A+1cos⁡A+sin⁡A−1=(cos⁡A−sin⁡A+1)(cos⁡A+sin⁡A+1)(cos⁡A+sin⁡A−1)(cos⁡A+sin⁡A+1)\dfrac{\cos A - \sin A + 1}{\cos A + \sin A - 1} = \dfrac{(\cos A - \sin A + 1)(\cos A + \sin A + 1)}{(\cos A + \sin A - 1)(\cos A + \sin A + 1)}cosA+sinA−1cosA−sinA+1​=(cosA+sinA−1)(cosA+sinA+1)(cosA−sinA+1)(cosA+sinA+1)​

=cos⁡2A+2cos⁡A+1−sin⁡2A2sin⁡Acos⁡A= \dfrac{\cos^2 A + 2\cos A + 1 - \sin^2 A}{2\sin A\cos A}=2sinAcosAcos2A+2cosA+1−sin2A​

Question: The distance between the points (cos⁡30°,sin⁡30°)(\cos 30°, \sin 30°)(cos30°,sin30°) and (cos⁡60°,−sin⁡60°)(\cos 60°, -\sin 60°)(cos60°,−sin60°) is

Given: two points with table values as coordinates. Asked: the distance between them.

Concept used: table values (Topic 4), then the distance formula (Chapter 7). Why it applies: after substituting, the points have ordinary coordinates.

  1. 1

    Substitute: P(32,12)P\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2}\right)P(23​​,21​) and Q(12,−32)Q\left(\dfrac{1}{2}, -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)Q(21​,−23​​).

  2. 2

    Distance formula.

    PQ2=(12−32)2+(−32−12)2PQ^2 = \left(\dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2 + \left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2PQ2=(21​−23​​)2+(−23​​−21​)2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Expand each square: (1−3)24=4−234\dfrac{(1 - \sqrt{3})^2}{4} = \dfrac{4 - 2\sqrt{3}}{4}4(1−3​)2​=44−23​​ and (3+1)24=4+234\dfrac{(\sqrt{3} + 1)^2}{4} = \dfrac{4 + 2\sqrt{3}}{4}4(3​+1)2​=44+23​​.

    PQ2=4−234+4+234PQ^2 = \dfrac{4 - 2\sqrt{3}}{4} + \dfrac{4 + 2\sqrt{3}}{4}PQ2=44−23​​+44+23​​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Add (the 3\sqrt{3}3​ terms cancel).

    PQ2=84=2PQ^2 = \dfrac{8}{4} = 2PQ2=48​=2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Take the square root.

    PQ=2PQ = \sqrt{2}PQ=2​Swipe to see the whole equation →

  6. Check: both points are 1 unit from the origin, and the angle between them at the origin is 90° (one at 30° above the x-axis, one at 60° below), so PQ is the diagonal of a unit square: 2\sqrt{2}2​ ✔.

    Why the other options are wrong: A, B and C do not come from any correct working. Forgetting the minus sign on sin⁡60°\sin 60°sin60° gives 2−3≈0.52\sqrt{2 - \sqrt{3}} \approx 0.522−3​​≈0.52, which is not even an option — a sign that something has gone wrong.
    Common trap: Dropping the minus sign in −sin⁡60°-\sin 60°−sin60°.
D. 2\sqrt{2}2​ units: distance =(12−32)2+(12+32)2=2= \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2} = \sqrt{2}=(21​−23​​)2+(21​+23​​)2​=2​

Question: Which one of the following is not equal to Unity?
A. sin⁡2x+cos⁡2x\sin^2 x + \cos^2 xsin2x+cos2x
B. cot⁡2x−cosec⁡2x\cot^2 x - \operatorname{cosec}^2 xcot2x−cosec2x
C. sec⁡2x−tan⁡2x\sec^2 x - \tan^2 xsec2x−tan2x
D. tan⁡x⋅cot⁡x\tan x \cdot \cot xtanx⋅cotx

Given: four expressions. Asked: the one that is not 1.

Concept used: the identities in their rearranged forms (Topic 5). Why it applies: three options are identities equal to 1.

  1. 1

    A: sin⁡2x+cos⁡2x=1\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1sin2x+cos2x=1 (first identity).

  2. 2

    B: cosec⁡2x−cot⁡2x=1\operatorname{cosec}^2 x - \cot^2 x = 1cosec2x−cot2x=1, so cot⁡2x−cosec⁡2x=−1\cot^2 x - \operatorname{cosec}^2 x = -1cot2x−cosec2x=−1. Not 1.

  3. 3

    C: sec⁡2x−tan⁡2x=1\sec^2 x - \tan^2 x = 1sec2x−tan2x=1.

  4. 4

    D: tan and cot are reciprocals, so tan⁡xcot⁡x=1\tan x\cot x = 1tanxcotx=1.

  5. Check: at x = 45°: B gives 1−2=−11 - 2 = -11−2=−1 ✔.

    Common trap: Not noticing the order in B — it is the negative of the identity.
B. cot⁡2x−cosec⁡2x=−1\cot^2 x - \operatorname{cosec}^2 x = -1cot2x−cosec2x=−1, so it is not equal to unity

Question: Prove that: (sin⁡x−cos⁡x+1)⋅(sec⁡x−tan⁡x)=(sin⁡x+cos⁡x−1)(\sin x - \cos x + 1)\cdot(\sec x - \tan x) = (\sin x + \cos x - 1)(sinx−cosx+1)⋅(secx−tanx)=(sinx+cosx−1)

Given: the identity. To prove: LHS = RHS.

Concept used: Move 1 (sec⁡x−tan⁡x=1−sin⁡xcos⁡x\sec x - \tan x = \dfrac{1 - \sin x}{\cos x}secx−tanx=cosx1−sinx​), then expand and use Move 4 (1−sin⁡2x=cos⁡2x1 - \sin^2 x = \cos^2 x1−sin2x=cos2x) (Topic 6). Why it applies: grouping (1+sin⁡x)(1 + \sin x)(1+sinx) in the first bracket makes (1+sin⁡x)(1−sin⁡x)(1 + \sin x)(1 - \sin x)(1+sinx)(1−sinx) appear.

  1. 1

    Start from the LHS.

    LHS=(sin⁡x−cos⁡x+1)(sec⁡x−tan⁡x)\text{LHS} = (\sin x - \cos x + 1)(\sec x - \tan x)LHS=(sinx−cosx+1)(secx−tanx)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Move 1.

    =(sin⁡x−cos⁡x+1)(1−sin⁡xcos⁡x)= (\sin x - \cos x + 1)\left(\dfrac{1 - \sin x}{\cos x}\right)=(sinx−cosx+1)(cosx1−sinx​)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Regroup the first bracket as (1+sin⁡x)−cos⁡x(1 + \sin x) - \cos x(1+sinx)−cosx and multiply each part.

    =(1+sin⁡x)(1−sin⁡xcos⁡x)−cos⁡x(1−sin⁡xcos⁡x)= (1 + \sin x)\left(\dfrac{1 - \sin x}{\cos x}\right) - \cos x\left(\dfrac{1 - \sin x}{\cos x}\right)=(1+sinx)(cosx1−sinx​)−cosx(cosx1−sinx​)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    First part: (1+sin⁡x)(1−sin⁡x)=1−sin⁡2x(1 + \sin x)(1 - \sin x) = 1 - \sin^2 x(1+sinx)(1−sinx)=1−sin2x. Second part: cancel cos⁡x\cos xcosx.

    =1−sin⁡2xcos⁡x−(1−sin⁡x)= \dfrac{1 - \sin^2 x}{\cos x} - (1 - \sin x)=cosx1−sin2x​−(1−sinx)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Move 4: 1−sin⁡2x=cos⁡2x1 - \sin^2 x = \cos^2 x1−sin2x=cos2x.

    =cos⁡2xcos⁡x−1+sin⁡x= \dfrac{\cos^2 x}{\cos x} - 1 + \sin x=cosxcos2x​−1+sinxSwipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Cancel and reorder.

    =sin⁡x+cos⁡x−1=RHS= \sin x + \cos x - 1 = \text{RHS}=sinx+cosx−1=RHSSwipe to see the whole equation →

  7. Hence proved.

    Check: at x = 60°: LHS =(32−12+1)(2−3)=3+12(2−3)=3−12= \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2} + 1\right)(2 - \sqrt{3}) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3} + 1}{2}(2 - \sqrt{3}) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3} - 1}{2}=(23​​−21​+1)(2−3​)=23​+1​(2−3​)=23​−1​; RHS =32+12−1=3−12= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2} - 1 = \dfrac{\sqrt{3} - 1}{2}=23​​+21​−1=23​−1​ ✔.
